title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 First Paper: Network Reconfiguration in Distribution Systems for Loss Reduction and Demand Balancing, Baran et. al.
In this document, I review two papers. The first papers introduces the derivation is for three-phase, balanced systems. The second derviation is for three-phase unbalanced systems.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.2 Paper’s Objectives
1- How can we change the network configuration to reduce resistive losses? 2- How can the load be distributed such that no overloads occur on the T-Lines?

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.1 Deriving the Real and Reactive Power Equations
NOTE: Baran and Wu use the DistFlow equations for a balanced, single-phase equivalent radial distribution system. We use these equations as a starting point for our unbalanced three-phase work.
Consider the following single line diagram:
For each load, we consider \(P_{L,n}\) and \(Q_{L,n}\), indicating real and reactive power consumed at bus \(n\). Positive load means consumption.
Each line has an impedance, \(\bar{Z}_{n} = r_{n}+jx_{n}\). The sending-end complex power flow on each line is given by:
\[\bar{S}_{n} = P_{n}+jQ_{n}\]
For instance, for the line leaving bus \(i+1\):
\[\bar{S}_{i+1} = P_{i+1}+jQ_{i+1}\]
I think it is easier to see this if we look at the power flow between two consecutive buses. Consider the power flow between buses \(n\) and \(n+1\). We define \(P_n\) as the power leaving bus \(n\) and entering line \((n,n+1)\):
\[\underbrace{P_{n}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{P_{n,loss}}_{\text{Line loss}} + \underbrace{P_{n+1}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n+1$}} + \underbrace{P_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Load at bus $n+1$}} \tag{4.1}\]

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.1.1 Decomposing the Losses term in equation Equation 4.1
\[P_{loss} = r |I|^{2}\]
At any given bus \(n\):
\[P_{n,loss} = r_{n} |I_{n}|^{2} \tag{4.2}\]
Recall:
\[\bar{S} = \bar{V}\bar{I}^{*} = P+jQ\]
Wherein the magnitude of the apparent power is given by:
\[|S| = |I|~|V| = \sqrt{P^{2} + Q^{2}}\]
Squaring both sides:
\[|S|^{2} = |I|^{2}~|V|^{2} = P^{2}+Q^{2}\]
Solving for the squared current magnitude:
\[|I|^{2} = \frac{P^{2} + Q^{2}}{|V|^{2}}\]
For the line leaving bus \(n\), the squared current magnitude is:
\[|I_{n}|^{2} = \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|V_{n}|^{2}} \tag{4.3}\]
substituting the current equation Equation 4.3 into Equation 4.2 we get:
\[P_{n,loss} = r_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}} \tag{4.4}\]
Substituting Equation 4.4 in the power balance between buses \(n\) and \(n+1\) in Equation 4.1, we get:
\[\underbrace{P_{n}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{r_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}}}_{\text{Line loss}} + \underbrace{P_{n+1}}_{\text{Power leaving bus $n+1$}} +\underbrace{P_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Load at bus $n+1$}} \tag{4.5}\]






NoteNote



Equation 4.5 is the real power DistFlow Equation. This is the exact branch real-power balance for the single-phase equivalent line model, assuming the bus has one downstream line and no additional injection. For a branching feeder, we also account for every outgoing branch.


Similarly, the reactive power can be calculated in a similar manner:
\[\underbrace{Q_{n}}_{\text{Q leaving bus $n$}} = \underbrace{x_{n} \frac{P^{2}_{n} + Q^{2}_{n}}{|\bar{V}_{n}|^{2}}}_{\text{Reactive power absorbed in the line}} + \underbrace{Q_{n+1}}_{\text{Q leaving bus $n+1$}} +\underbrace{Q_{L,n+1}}_{\text{Q consumed by bus $n+1$ load}} \tag{4.6}\]

title: 4  Equations Derivation
text:
4.2 Deriving the Voltage Equation:
Applying KVL to buses, \(i\) and \(i-1\) in Figure 4.1:
\[\bar{V}_{i-1} = \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} + \bar{V}_{i} \tag{4.7}\]
The current complex value can be solved for in a similar manner as in equation Equation 4.3:
\[\bar{V}_{n}~\bar{I}_{n}^{*} = P_{n}+jQ_{n}\]
Taking the complex conjugate and solving for \(\bar{I}_{n}\):
\[\bar{I}_{n} = \frac{P_{n}-jQ_{n}}{\bar{V}_{n}^{*}} \tag{4.8}\]
Substituting Equation 4.8 in Equation 4.7 & solving for \(\bar{V}_{i}\):
\[\bar{V}_{i} = \bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} \tag{4.9}\]
\[\bar{V}_{i} = \bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\frac{P_{i-1}-jQ_{i-1}}{\bar{V}_{i-1}^{*}}\]
We can then extend this to get only the magnitude of the voltage:
Recall \(|a-b|^{2} = (a-b)(a^{*}-b^{*})\):
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = (\bar{V}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1})~(\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1} - \bar{Z}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}^{*}_{i-1})\]
Multiplying both terms, we end up with:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2~\Re \{\underbrace{\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}}_{\substack{\text{Apparent} \\ \text {Power} \\ \text{Conjugate}}}~\bar{Z}_{i-1}\} + |\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2}~|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} \tag{4.10}\]
Recall \(\bar{S}^{*}_{i-1} = \bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1} = P_{i-1} - jQ_{i-1}\)
So the middle term can be decomposed such that:
\[\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}~\bar{Z}_{i-1} = (P_{i-1} - jQ_{i-1})(r_{i-1}+jx_{i-1})\]
Multiplying and obtaining only the real part because we are trying to calculate the magnitude:
\[\Re \{\bar{Z}_{i-1}~\bar{V}^{*}_{i-1}~\bar{I}_{i-1}\} = r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1} \tag{4.11}\]
The last term in Equation 4.10 can be simplified further. Recall that \(|\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2} = r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1}\) and \(|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} = \frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}}\)
\[|\bar{Z}_{i-1}|^{2}~|\bar{I}_{i-1}|^{2} = (r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1})~(\frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}}) \tag{4.12}\]
Substituting Equation 4.11 and Equation 4.12 in Equation 4.10:
\[|\bar{V}_{i}|^{2} = |\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2} - 2(r_{i-1}~P_{i-1} + x_{i-1}~Q_{i-1})+(r^{2}_{i-1} + x^{2}_{i-1})~\frac{P^{2}_{i-1}+Q^{2}_{i-1}}{|\bar{V}_{i-1}|^{2}} \tag{4.13}\]






NoteNote



Equation 4.13 is the Voltage Magnitude DistFlow Equation. This equation applies exactly to each branch under the paper’s single-phase equivalent series-impedance model. It does not, by itself, describe mutual coupling in an unbalanced three-phase system.

title: 3  Background Information
text:
3.1 Three-phase Branch Power Matrix
NOTE: This file contains supporting matrix algebra and the fuller multiphase branch-flow formulation of Gan and Low (Gan and Low 2014). The working equations are in ch2_voltage_reactive_equations.qmd.
Recall that \(\mathbf{\bar V}_i\) and \(\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\) are \(3\times1\) column vectors. We previously used the per-phase complex power vector:
\[\mathbf{\bar s}_{ij}=\begin{bmatrix}P_{ij}^a+jQ_{ij}^a\\P_{ij}^b+jQ_{ij}^b\\P_{ij}^c+jQ_{ij}^c\end{bmatrix}\]
Gan and Low also use the full branch power matrix:
\[\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^{H} \tag{3.1}\]
Expanding the matrix multiplication:
\[
\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^a(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*\\
\bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^b(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*\\
\bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^a)^* & \bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^b)^* & \bar V_i^c(\bar I_{ij}^c)^*
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Note that the diagonal elements are the conventional complex powers for each phase:
\[\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij})=\mathbf{\bar s}_{ij}\]
The off-diagonal elements are cross-phase voltage-current products. They do not represent extra downstream branches or separate real/reactive phase powers. The full \(3\times3\) matrix is useful for Gan and Low’s branch-flow and optimization formulations, but it is not required just to substitute phase power into KVL.

title: 3  Background Information
section: 3.2 Derive the Magnitude of the Voltage
text:
3.2 Derive the Magnitude of the Voltage
Following the same approach as in Equation 4.20, we can obtain squared voltage magnitudes using the three-phase KVL equation:
\[\mathbf{\bar V}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\]
To retain all cross-phase voltage products, multiply the equation on the right by its Hermitian transpose:
\[\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^H=(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})^H \tag{3.2}\]
The Hermitian transpose, denoted by \(H\), means conjugate transpose; it does not mean extracting the diagonal. A \(3\times1\) voltage vector times its \(1\times3\) conjugate transpose produces a \(3\times3\) matrix.

3.2.1 Solving for the left hand side of Equation 3.2
\[
\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^{H}
=\begin{bmatrix}\bar V_j^a\\\bar V_j^b\\\bar V_j^c\end{bmatrix}_{3\times1}
\begin{bmatrix}(\bar V_j^a)^*&(\bar V_j^b)^*&(\bar V_j^c)^*\end{bmatrix}_{1\times3}
=\begin{bmatrix}
|\bar V_j^a|^2&\bar V_j^a(\bar V_j^b)^*&\bar V_j^a(\bar V_j^c)^*\\
\bar V_j^b(\bar V_j^a)^*&|\bar V_j^b|^2&\bar V_j^b(\bar V_j^c)^*\\
\bar V_j^c(\bar V_j^a)^*&\bar V_j^c(\bar V_j^b)^*&|\bar V_j^c|^2
\end{bmatrix}_{3\times3}
\tag{3.3}\]
Note that the diagonal elements are squared voltage magnitudes. The off-diagonal elements remain complex cross-phase voltage products.
Gan and Low define the voltage matrix as:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_j\mathbf{\bar V}_j^H \tag{3.4}\]
Similarly:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_i=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H \tag{3.5}\]


3.2.2 Solving for the right hand side of Equation 3.2
We can apply the same Hermitian transpose to the right-hand side:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=(\mathbf{\bar V}_i-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij})(\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H-\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H)\]






NoteVoltage Eq. Note



\[(\mathbf{\bar Z}\mathbf{\bar I})^H=\mathbf{\bar I}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}^H\]
The multiplication order reverses because \((AB)^H=B^HA^H\). This is a property of the conjugate transpose, not merely a rule for fixing dimensions.


Expanding the right-hand side:
\[\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H-\mathbf{\bar V}_i\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar V}_i^H+\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H \tag{3.6}\]
We previously defined the voltage matrix in Equation 3.5 and the branch-power matrix in Equation 3.1. Accordingly, we can define the current outer-product matrix as:
\[\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}=\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar I}_{ij}^H\]
Therefore, Equation 3.6 can be written as:
\[\boxed{\mathbf{\bar W}_j=\mathbf{\bar W}_i-\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H-\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar S}_{ij}^H+\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H} \tag{3.7}\]






NoteNote



Equation 3.7 is an exact squared-voltage matrix relationship derived from KVL. The term \(\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar L}_{ij}\mathbf{\bar Z}_{ij}^H\) is quadratic in line current; it is the outer product of the line voltage-drop vector with itself. Its diagonal is not the same as the real-power loss. For our immediate voltage–reactive-power work, the per-phase power equations and KVL are sufficient as starting equations, so we can keep this fuller derivation for background.






Gan, Lingwen, and Steven H Low. 2014. “Convex Relaxations and Linear Approximation for Optimal Power Flow in Multiphase Radial Networks.” 2014 Power Systems Computation Conference, 1–9.
